front: Why do cells swell when oxidative phosphorylation fails?
back: ATP depletion impairs ion pumps, allowing intracellular sodium and water accumulation.
explanation: Reduced ATP impairs sodium-potassium pumps, causing sodium and water accumulation and potentially reversible swelling.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Can severe anemia cause tissue hypoxia with a normal arterial oxygen tension?
back: Yes. Reduced hemoglobin lowers blood oxygen content despite normal dissolved oxygen tension.
explanation: Most blood oxygen is carried by hemoglobin. Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen content despite normal saturation and dissolved oxygen tension.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What distinguishes ischemia from isolated hypoxemia at the tissue level?
back: Ischemia also reduces nutrient delivery and removal of metabolic waste.
explanation: Ischemia restricts both oxygen and substrate delivery and prevents clearance of metabolic products, limiting anaerobic compensation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why does intracellular pH fall during ischemic injury?
back: Anaerobic glycolysis increases lactate production as oxidative ATP generation fails.
explanation: Reduced oxygen availability impairs oxidative ATP production, increasing reliance on glycolysis and lactate formation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is the functional consequence of ribosomal detachment from rough ER during injury?
back: Reduced protein synthesis.
explanation: Ribosome detachment reduces translation, especially of proteins normally synthesized on rough endoplasmic reticulum.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Name three damaging enzyme classes activated by excess cytosolic calcium.
back: Phospholipases, endonucleases and ATPases.
explanation: Excess calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes, nucleases that damage DNA and ATPases that consume ATP.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which two major abnormalities characterize irreversible cell injury?
back: Inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction and severe membrane damage.
explanation: Failure to recover mitochondrial function together with severe membrane damage supports irreversible injury.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why do serum intracellular enzymes rise after necrotic tissue injury?
back: Damaged plasma membranes allow intracellular proteins to leak into circulation.
explanation: Membrane disruption permits intracellular proteins to escape into extracellular fluid and circulation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why can the same agent cause reversible injury in one exposure and cell death in another?
back: Dose, duration, cellular susceptibility and repair capacity determine the outcome.
explanation: Injury outcome depends on the nature, severity and duration of the insult as well as cellular susceptibility and repair capacity.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does mitochondrial permeability transition impair ATP production?
back: It dissipates the inner-membrane electrochemical gradient required for oxidative phosphorylation.
explanation: Loss of the mitochondrial electrochemical gradient prevents ATP synthase from efficiently generating ATP.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does hypertrophy differ from cellular swelling?
back: Hypertrophy increases functional cellular substance; swelling primarily reflects excess intracellular water.
explanation: Increased workload stimulates synthesis of proteins and organelles, enlarging individual cardiomyocytes.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why can the liver undergo compensatory hyperplasia after partial resection?
back: Surviving hepatocytes retain the capacity to proliferate in response to growth signals.
explanation: Hepatocytes can re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate in response to growth signals after tissue loss.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What distinguishes hyperplasia from hypertrophy?
back: Hyperplasia increases cell number; hypertrophy increases individual cell size.
explanation: Estrogen can stimulate endometrial cell proliferation. Hyperplasia is distinct from invasion, although some forms confer increased cancer risk.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What happens to protein balance during disuse atrophy?
back: Protein synthesis falls and degradation rises, reducing cell size.
explanation: Reduced workload shifts protein balance toward loss of cellular substance, producing disuse atrophy.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How can loss of hormonal stimulation produce tissue atrophy?
back: Reduced trophic signals lower cellular activity and promote loss of cell size and sometimes number.
explanation: Withdrawal of hormonal support reduces tissue activity and promotes atrophy.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What functional cost accompanies squamous metaplasia in bronchial epithelium?
back: Loss of normal mucociliary clearance despite greater resistance to irritation.
explanation: Persistent irritation can reprogram progenitor cells toward a more resistant mature epithelial phenotype.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What makes Barrett esophagus an example of metaplasia?
back: The normal squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium.
explanation: Replacement of one mature epithelial type by another is metaplasia; in this setting it is Barrett esophagus.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Is metaplasia necessarily permanent?
back: No. It may regress after removal of the persistent stimulus.
explanation: Metaplastic epithelial populations can be replaced by the normal phenotype when persistent stress resolves.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does autophagy participate in atrophy?
back: It degrades and recycles organelles and other cellular components through lysosomes.
explanation: Autophagy delivers cellular components to lysosomes for degradation and reuse, contributing to adaptation during atrophy.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why can pathological hypertrophy eventually fail to preserve function?
back: Persistent demand may exceed the enlarged cells’ metabolic and perfusion capacity.
explanation: Hypertrophy initially helps meet workload, but sustained stress can outstrip perfusion and cellular capacity and contribute to dysfunction.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is karyolysis?
back: Fading and dissolution of nuclear staining as DNA is degraded.
explanation: Karyolysis is fading or dissolution of nuclear material due to DNA degradation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How do pyknosis and karyorrhexis differ?
back: Pyknosis is nuclear condensation; karyorrhexis is nuclear fragmentation.
explanation: Pyknosis describes nuclear shrinkage and chromatin condensation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why does necrotic cytoplasm often become more eosinophilic?
back: Protein denaturation increases eosin binding, and loss of RNA reduces basophilia.
explanation: Denatured proteins bind eosin more strongly, while loss of basophilic RNA reduces the blue cytoplasmic component.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which initiator caspase is associated with the mitochondrial apoptotic pathway?
back: Caspase-9, activated through the apoptosome.
explanation: Cytochrome c associates with APAF-1 to form the apoptosome, activating the initiator caspase of the intrinsic pathway.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which apoptotic pathway is initiated by Fas-Fas ligand binding?
back: The extrinsic death-receptor pathway, involving caspase-8.
explanation: Fas signaling activates the extrinsic apoptotic pathway through adaptor proteins and initiator caspase-8.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does BCL-2 inhibit the intrinsic apoptotic pathway?
back: It opposes mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release.
explanation: Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins oppose BAX/BAK-mediated mitochondrial membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why does apoptosis usually provoke less inflammation than necrosis?
back: Membrane-bound fragments are rapidly cleared, limiting leakage of intracellular contents.
explanation: Packaging into apoptotic bodies and prompt phagocytosis limit exposure of inflammatory intracellular contents.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which membrane lipid becomes externalized as an apoptotic clearance signal?
back: Phosphatidylserine.
explanation: Externalized phosphatidylserine acts as an eat-me signal during apoptotic clearance.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Can apoptosis occur without disease?
back: Yes. It is essential in development and normal tissue homeostasis.
explanation: Apoptosis participates in normal developmental sculpting as well as pathological cell removal.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What links necrotic membrane rupture to inflammation?
back: Released intracellular damage-associated molecules activate innate immune responses.
explanation: Necrotic membrane disruption exposes intracellular molecules that activate innate inflammatory responses.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which necrosis pattern is typical of an ischemic splenic infarct?
back: Coagulative necrosis.
explanation: Ischemic death in most solid organs produces coagulative necrosis, with temporary preservation of tissue architecture.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why does a cerebral infarct often leave a cavity?
back: Liquefactive necrosis digests the dead tissue.
explanation: Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis, in which enzymatic digestion removes the dead tissue.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What necrosis pattern commonly occurs in a bacterial abscess?
back: Liquefactive necrosis caused by enzymatic tissue digestion.
explanation: Enzymatic digestion by leukocytes and damaged cells produces liquefaction and purulent debris.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What combination suggests caseous necrosis?
back: Cheese-like gross material and granular acellular debris, often within a granuloma.
explanation: Caseous necrosis has a characteristic cheese-like gross appearance and granular acellular debris microscopically.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is saponification in fat necrosis?
back: Formation of calcium soaps when calcium binds fatty acids released from damaged adipocytes.
explanation: Lipases release fatty acids from damaged fat; calcium binds them to form soaps, a process called saponification.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Can fat necrosis occur without pancreatitis?
back: Yes. Trauma to adipose tissue, such as the breast, can cause it.
explanation: Mechanical injury to adipose tissue can produce fat necrosis with inflammation, fibrosis and calcification, mimicking a mass.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Where is fibrinoid necrosis characteristically found?
back: In vessel walls after certain immune-mediated or severe vascular injuries.
explanation: Severe vascular injury can produce fibrin-like eosinophilic deposits in vessel walls, termed fibrinoid necrosis.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What necrosis pattern underlies dry gangrene?
back: Predominantly coagulative necrosis from ischemia.
explanation: Dry gangrene is a clinical description of extensive ischemic tissue death, usually dominated by coagulative necrosis.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does wet gangrene differ from dry gangrene?
back: Infection and liquefactive digestion are superimposed on ischemic necrosis.
explanation: Superimposed infection adds leukocyte- and bacterial-enzyme-mediated digestion to ischemic tissue death, producing wet gangrene.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Does calcification of necrotic tissue require elevated serum calcium?
back: No. Dystrophic calcification can occur with normal serum calcium.
explanation: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or dead tissue without requiring hypercalcemia.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What defines macrovesicular steatosis?
back: A large intracellular triglyceride vacuole that often displaces the nucleus.
explanation: Macrovesicular steatosis is accumulation of neutral triglyceride within hepatocytes; lipid dissolves during routine processing.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why are frozen sections useful when demonstrating intracellular fat?
back: Routine processing dissolves lipid; frozen sections preserve it for lipid stains.
explanation: Frozen sections preserve lipid, allowing stains such as Oil Red O to demonstrate neutral fat.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What causes protein reabsorption droplets in proximal tubular cells?
back: Endocytosis of an excessive filtered protein load.
explanation: Proximal tubular cells reabsorb filtered proteins; a large protein load produces visible reabsorption droplets.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What are Russell bodies made of?
back: Retained immunoglobulin within plasma-cell rough endoplasmic reticulum.
explanation: Russell bodies represent immunoglobulin accumulation within dilated rough endoplasmic reticulum of plasma cells.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which stain helps identify hemosiderin?
back: Prussian blue, which demonstrates ferric iron.
explanation: Macrophages degrade erythrocytes and can store the released iron as hemosiderin, demonstrated by Prussian blue staining.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is lipofuscin, and does its presence alone prove severe dysfunction?
back: A residual lipid-protein pigment associated with aging; its presence alone does not prove major dysfunction.
explanation: Lipofuscin is a residual lysosomal pigment containing oxidized lipid and protein components and accumulates with age.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Where can inhaled carbon particles accumulate?
back: In pulmonary macrophages and draining hilar lymph nodes.
explanation: Inhaled carbon can be taken up by pulmonary macrophages and transported to draining lymph nodes, producing anthracotic pigment.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How can a protein-folding defect cause intracellular accumulation?
back: The abnormal protein may be retained rather than correctly transported or secreted.
explanation: Misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin can be retained in hepatocytes instead of being efficiently secreted; reduced circulating protein also affects the lung.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is the central accumulation mechanism in many lysosomal storage diseases?
back: A deficient degradative enzyme allows its substrate to accumulate within lysosomes.
explanation: Lysosomal storage diseases result when deficient catabolic enzymes permit their substrates to accumulate.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What gives atherosclerotic macrophages their foamy appearance?
back: Accumulated lipid, especially cholesterol esters.
explanation: Macrophages can accumulate cholesterol esters; dissolved cholesterol crystals leave clefts during tissue processing.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What common protein structure defines amyloid despite its different precursors?
back: Extracellular fibrils with a cross-beta-sheet structure.
explanation: Amyloid proteins have different precursors but adopt an ordered beta-sheet fibrillar structure, explaining their shared staining properties.

references.title: UCL National Amyloidosis Centre — Histology and proteomic analysis

front: Which amyloid precursor is produced by a clonal plasma-cell population?
back: Immunoglobulin light chains form AL amyloid.
explanation: The combination suggests AL amyloidosis; a plasma-cell clone produces the light-chain precursor. Tissue typing is still needed to confirm the amyloid type.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: What protein is the precursor of AA amyloid?
back: Serum amyloid A, a hepatic acute-phase protein.
explanation: Chronic inflammation increases hepatic production of the acute-phase protein SAA, from which AA fibrils are derived.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: Which precursor causes dialysis-related amyloid in joints and tendons?
back: Beta-2 microglobulin.
explanation: Reduced renal clearance and incomplete removal during dialysis permit beta-2 microglobulin accumulation, especially in osteoarticular tissues.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: What does a pathogenic TTR variant cause?
back: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv).
explanation: A pathogenic TTR variant can destabilize transthyretin and cause hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, or both.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: Why does a monoclonal serum protein not establish AL amyloidosis by itself?
back: It may coexist with another amyloid type; the deposited protein must be typed.
explanation: Proteomic analysis identifies the deposited protein. A monoclonal protein alone does not prove AL because monoclonal gammopathy can coexist with other amyloid types.

references.title: UCL National Amyloidosis Centre — Histology and proteomic analysis

front: How does glomerular amyloid cause nephrotic edema?
back: Albuminuria lowers plasma oncotic pressure; renal sodium retention also contributes.
explanation: Glomerular deposition disrupts filtration barrier selectivity, allowing albumin loss and producing nephrotic syndrome.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: Does a negative abdominal fat biopsy rule out amyloidosis?
back: No. Sensitivity varies, and tissue deposits can be patchy.
explanation: Deposits can be patchy and screening-biopsy sensitivity varies by amyloid type. Further subtype-appropriate evaluation or involved-organ biopsy may be needed.

references.title: UCL — Amyloidosis: histologic diagnosis and biopsy sensitivity

front: Why does controlling chronic inflammation help prevent AA deposition?
back: It lowers production of the precursor serum amyloid A.
explanation: Reducing inflammation lowers the supply of SAA, the precursor for AA fibrils. This targets new precursor production rather than instantly removing existing deposits.

references.title: NIDDK — Amyloidosis and Kidney Disease

front: Is amyloid principally an intracellular or extracellular deposit?
back: Extracellular.
explanation: Amyloid is an extracellular protein deposit; its location distinguishes it from intracellular storage inclusions.

references.title: UCL National Amyloidosis Centre — Histology and proteomic analysis

front: What potentially harmful product remains after superoxide dismutase acts?
back: Hydrogen peroxide, which still needs detoxification.
explanation: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen; peroxide then requires removal by catalase or peroxidases.

references.title: Superoxide dismutase–catalase conjugates: peroxide and Fenton reaction

front: Which peroxisomal enzyme converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen?
back: Catalase.
explanation: Catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen, limiting peroxide availability for radical formation.

references.title: Catalase-deficient mice and oxidant injury

front: Why can free iron worsen peroxide-mediated injury?
back: It catalyzes formation of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals.
explanation: Redox-active ferrous iron reacts with peroxide in Fenton chemistry, generating highly reactive hydroxyl radicals near cellular targets.

references.title: Fenton reaction products and cellular differentiation or death

front: What membrane process propagates radical injury after the initiating event?
back: Lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids.
explanation: Radical attack initiates a chain reaction in membrane lipids, compromising membrane structure and producing reactive breakdown products.

references.title: NIEHS — Cellular and tissue responses to toxicity

front: What does glutathione peroxidase consume when reducing peroxides?
back: Reduced glutathione (GSH), producing oxidized glutathione (GSSG).
explanation: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione as an electron donor; glutathione becomes oxidized as peroxide is reduced.

references.title: Antioxidant enzymes in human cells and tissues

front: What reactive species does phagocyte NADPH oxidase initially generate?
back: Superoxide anion.
explanation: Phagocyte NADPH oxidase transfers electrons to oxygen to generate superoxide, initiating microbicidal oxidant production.

references.title: NIH — NADPH oxidase correction in chronic granulomatous disease

front: Why can oxygen restoration worsen an ischemic tissue injury?
back: Reperfusion can generate ROS and amplify calcium overload and inflammation.
explanation: Returning oxygen can fuel oxidant formation in injured cells and recruited leukocytes; calcium overload and inflammation also contribute to reperfusion injury.

references.title: NIEHS — Cellular and tissue responses to toxicity

front: How can ionizing radiation injure DNA indirectly?
back: Water radiolysis generates radicals that attack DNA.
explanation: Ionizing radiation can split water and generate radicals that subsequently injure DNA and other molecules; scavenging reduces this indirect component.

references.title: NIEHS — Cellular and tissue responses to toxicity

front: How can ROS reduce enzyme activity without reducing protein quantity?
back: They oxidize side chains and alter folding or cross-linking.
explanation: Oxidation can alter active sites, folding, and intermolecular interactions, impairing function even when the amount of protein is unchanged.

references.title: NIEHS — Cellular and tissue responses to toxicity

front: Why does iron sequestration reduce oxidative injury?
back: It limits the labile iron available to catalyze radical formation.
explanation: Safely storing iron limits iron-catalyzed radical formation; total iron content alone does not measure the reactive iron pool.

references.title: Ferritin mineralization and iron storage

front: Why can severe anemia cause hypoxia despite normal PaO2?
back: There is less hemoglobin available to carry oxygen.
explanation: Most blood oxygen is hemoglobin-bound; normal saturation cannot compensate for markedly reduced hemoglobin.

references.title: NCBI Bookshelf — Oxygen transport in normal and pathological situations

front: What does ischemia impair besides oxygen delivery?
back: Nutrient delivery and clearance of metabolic waste.
explanation: Low blood flow restricts glucose delivery and removal of acidic metabolites as well as oxygen delivery.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does carbon monoxide impair hemoglobin-mediated oxygen delivery?
back: It occupies oxygen-binding sites and impairs oxygen release from the remaining sites.
explanation: Carbon monoxide occupies hemoglobin and increases oxygen affinity at remaining sites.

references.title: UK Health Security Agency — Carbon monoxide toxicological overview

front: What type of hypoxia results from cyanide inhibition of complex IV?
back: Histotoxic hypoxia: cells cannot adequately use delivered oxygen.
explanation: Cytochrome c oxidase inhibition blocks electron transport and oxygen-dependent ATP generation.

references.title: Clinical features and management of cyanide poisoning

front: What connects ATP depletion to hydropic cell swelling?
back: Ion-pump failure causes intracellular sodium and water accumulation.
explanation: Intracellular sodium accumulation draws water into the cell.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which two enzyme groups link calcium overload to membrane and cytoskeletal damage?
back: Phospholipases and proteases.
explanation: These enzymes damage membranes and structural proteins, amplifying injury.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What cellular event allows necrotic-cell proteins to appear in blood?
back: Loss of plasma-membrane integrity permits leakage.
explanation: Damaged membranes allow intracellular proteins to escape.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Can infection injure tissue through the host response rather than direct pathogen destruction?
back: Yes. Antigen-specific immune cells can kill infected host cells.
explanation: Antigen-specific T cells can eliminate infected cells through cytotoxic pathways.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How can crushing injury initiate cell damage?
back: Direct mechanical disruption of cells, often compounded by impaired perfusion.
explanation: Crushing directly damages cells; secondary ischemia can amplify that injury.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What two major abnormalities strongly support irreversible injury?
back: Failure to recover mitochondrial function and severe membrane damage.
explanation: Persistent inability to restore mitochondrial function with severe membrane damage supports irreversible injury.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What remains temporarily recognizable in coagulative necrosis?
back: The tissue architecture, despite loss of viable cells and nuclei.
explanation: Protein denaturation initially preserves the framework of an ischemic solid-organ infarct.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which necrosis pattern characterizes an ischemic brain infarct?
back: Liquefactive necrosis.
explanation: Enzymatic digestion of infarcted brain produces liquefaction and eventual cavitation.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why do many bacterial abscesses show liquefactive necrosis?
back: Leukocyte and microbial enzymes digest the involved tissue.
explanation: Hydrolytic enzymes liquefy tissue within a bacterial abscess.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What is the classic necrotic pattern within a tuberculous granuloma?
back: Caseous necrosis.
explanation: Tuberculous granulomas commonly contain central caseous material.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What chemical process makes enzymatic fat necrosis look chalky?
back: Saponification: calcium salts form from released fatty acids.
explanation: Saponification follows enzymatic fat destruction.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Where is fibrinoid necrosis typically recognized?
back: In damaged blood-vessel walls, often in immune-mediated vascular injury.
explanation: This pattern describes intensely eosinophilic vessel-wall injury containing fibrin-like material.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Why does apoptosis usually provoke less inflammation than necrosis?
back: Cell contents are packaged and promptly cleared before extensive leakage.
explanation: Apoptotic fragments are packaged and removed before substantial leakage.

references.title: Molecular Biology of the Cell — Programmed Cell Death

front: What cytosolic mitochondrial protein helps assemble the apoptosome?
back: Cytochrome c.
explanation: Mitochondrial cytochrome c release initiates apoptosome-dependent caspase activation.

references.title: Molecular Biology of the Cell — Programmed Cell Death

front: Which apoptotic pathway is initiated by Fas engagement?
back: The extrinsic death-receptor pathway.
explanation: Fas ligation triggers the extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway.

references.title: Molecular Biology of the Cell — Programmed Cell Death

front: How do pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis differ?
back: Nuclear condensation, nuclear fragmentation, and fading/dissolution, respectively.
explanation: Karyorrhexis is fragmentation of a condensed nucleus.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which highly reactive radical can arise when ionizing radiation interacts with cellular water?
back: The hydroxyl radical.
explanation: Water radiolysis can generate highly reactive hydroxyl radicals that damage nearby cellular molecules.

references.title: Mechanisms and Morphology of Cellular Injury, Adaptation, and Death

front: What is the degradative destination of many polyubiquitin-tagged cytosolic proteins?
back: The 26S proteasome.
explanation: Polyubiquitin can direct selected proteins to ATP-dependent proteasomal degradation.

references.title: The Cell — Protein Degradation

front: What are the products of superoxide dismutase activity?
back: Hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen.
explanation: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen.

references.title: Mechanisms and Morphology of Cellular Injury, Adaptation, and Death

front: Name three contributors to ischemia-reperfusion injury.
back: Reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, and inflammation.
explanation: Reoxygenation can add oxidative, calcium-mediated, and inflammatory damage to the original ischemic insult.

references.title: Mechanisms and Morphology of Cellular Injury, Adaptation, and Death

front: What distinguishes cardiomyocyte hypertrophy from hyperplasia?
back: Hypertrophy increases individual cardiomyocyte size; hyperplasia increases cell number.
explanation: Pressure-loaded cardiomyocytes adapt predominantly by increasing cell size.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which adaptive process increases hepatocyte number after partial hepatectomy?
back: Compensatory hyperplasia.
explanation: Division of surviving hepatocytes increases their number after tissue loss.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: What protective airway function is lost when ciliated epithelium becomes squamous?
back: Mucociliary clearance.
explanation: Squamous replacement may tolerate irritation but loses specialized ciliary clearance.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: How does ferritin help limit iron-mediated oxidative reactions?
back: It sequesters iron in an intracellular storage complex.
explanation: Ferritin sequesters iron in a storage complex, limiting freely available iron.

references.title: Ferritin and haemosiderin in free radical generation, lipid peroxidation and protein damage

front: What does lipofuscin represent in long-lived cells?
back: Residual, incompletely degraded material associated with cumulative cellular wear.
explanation: Lipofuscin is a residual pigment associated with cumulative intracellular wear and oxidative damage.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity

front: Which pigment in macrophages after hemorrhage is Prussian blue positive?
back: Hemosiderin.
explanation: Hemosiderin is an iron-containing storage pigment that gives a positive iron stain.

references.title: NIEHS — Basic Cellular and Tissue Microscopic Responses to Toxicity
